subject: Culture
title: Día de los Muertos
description: One-minute skill: Día de los Muertos.

hook.text: On November 2, Mexican families picnic on graves, play music, and leave tequila for the dead. It's a party.

buildup.text: Día de los Muertos blends Aztec death worship with Catholic All Saints' Day. The dead return for one night.

discovery.text: Altars called 'ofrendas' hold photos, marigolds, candles, and the deceased's favorite foods. Every item has meaning.

twist.text: Octavio Paz wrote that Mexicans laugh at death while Americans hide from it. The attitudes reveal opposing fears.

climax.text: The holiday's global popularity surged after Pixar's 'Coco.' Pop culture introduced ancestral reverence to millions.

punchline.text: Death is not the opposite of life—it's part of the same story.

quiz.question: What are the home altars for Día de los Muertos called?

details.summary: Día de los Muertos is Mexico's vibrant celebration where the dead are honored with marigold-covered altars, sugar skulls, and favorite foods. Far from morbid, it is a joyful reunion where families welcome spirits back for one night, blending Aztec death worship with Catholic traditions.
details.whyItMatters: Día de los Muertos shows that grief and celebration can coexist. Its approach to death — joyful, communal, and ongoing — offers a powerful alternative to Western death avoidance.
takeaways: Día de los Muertos blends Aztec and Catholic death traditions
Ofrendas (altars) guide spirits home with marigolds, food, and photos
The holiday is a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

faq.question: Is Día de los Muertos the same as Halloween?
faq.answer: No. While both fall around November 1-2 and involve death imagery, they are distinct traditions. Día de los Muertos is a celebration of specific deceased loved ones, centered on family altars and cemetery visits. Halloween evolved from Celtic Samhain and focuses on fear, costumes, and candy.

faq.question: What is placed on an ofrenda?
faq.answer: Ofrendas include photos of the deceased, their favorite foods and drinks, marigold flowers (whose scent guides spirits), candles, incense (copal), sugar skulls, pan de muerto (bread of the dead), water, salt, and personal items the dead enjoyed.
